summary: Describes conventions for choosing the system identifier part of an NSAP address so it is unique inside a routing domain, to allow automatic configuration of TUBA/CLNP hosts. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Every house on a street needs a different number. This memo suggests how computers can pick their own number without anyone handing it out.

questions: system identifiers for tuba clnp hosts
how to assign unique addresses in osx networks
subtitle: How to assign unique addresses to computers transitioning to OSI networking

tldr.problem: TUBA and CLNP networks need to assign unique system identifiers within a routing domain and automatically configure addresses without manual intervention.
tldr.mechanism: Define conventions for the 6-octet system identifier field in NSAP addresses using either IEEE 802 addresses or embedded IP addresses, allowing systems to pick their own address without administrative assignment.
tldr.outcome: Computers can autoconfigure their full NSAP addresses by learning the area prefix from routers and inserting their own globally unique system identifier, enabling large-scale deployment without per-host configuration.

today: RFC 1526 is an Informational RFC describing conventions for a niche technology (TUBA/CLNP) that did not see widespread deployment. The Internet continued to use TCP/IP and later IPv6 rather than transitioning to OSI protocols. The mechanisms described here for autoconfiguration and globally unique identifiers influenced later address design, particularly in IPv6 and modern network management.

sections.title: Introduction to NSAP Addresses
sections.content:
NSAP (Network Service Access Point) addresses in OSI networks are structured like postal addresses: they route to a geographic or organizational region, then to a specific system, then to a port on that system. The address has an Initial Domain Part (IDP) that identifies the authority that assigned it, and a Domain Specific Part (DSP) that the authority defines internally.

The system identifier (often 6 octets or bytes) is the part of the DSP that must uniquely identify one computer within a routing domain. This memo proposes methods to assign these identifiers from globally managed sources (IEEE 802 addresses or Internet IP addresses) so computers can autoconfigure their addresses without manual intervention.
sections.eli5: Think of an NSAP address like a street address: the country, region, and building are set by authorities, but each computer needs its own unique 'house number' in the building. This explains how computers can pick their own number using Ethernet addresses or IP addresses, without anyone handing out numbers.

sections.title: The Structure of NSAP Addresses
sections.content:
An NSAP address is divided into hierarchical parts. The IDP contains the AFI (Authority and Format Identifier) and IDI (Initial Domain Identifier). The DSP is further split into High-Order DSP, system identifier (ID), and NSAP Selector. Both GOSIP Version 2 and ANSI standards define a 6-octet system identifier as the fixed length within their address formats, as shown in their respective address structure diagrams.

RFC 1237 specifies that the system identifier must be unique within an area for end systems and level 1 routers, and unique within the entire routing domain for level 2 routers. All gateways in a routing domain must use the same length for their system identifiers so routers can make efficient forwarding decisions.
sections.eli5: An NSAP address has several layers: the top tells you the country and organization, the middle parts tell you departments, and the bottom (the system identifier) identifies the specific computer. Everyone in the same organization must agree on how long the system identifier is so routers can find computers quickly.

sections.title: Autoconfiguration and Globally Unique Identifiers
sections.content:
A key goal for TUBA and CLNP networks is autoconfiguration: when an end system boots, it observes area addresses in IS-Hello packets sent by routers, then inserts its own system identifier to form its complete NSAP address. This requires the system identifier to be globally unique, so the same address cannot appear in two locations.

The memo clarifies a common misconception: the 6-octet system identifier does not have to be an IEEE 802 Ethernet address. Any globally unique identifier works. Using a uniform 6-octet length is chosen for efficiency, not because of Ethernet, although Ethernet addresses are one convenient source of global uniqueness.
sections.eli5: When a computer first turns on, it listens for routers to learn its area address, then adds its own unique identifier. The system identifier must be the same length everywhere so routers work efficiently. Ethernet addresses are convenient because they are already unique, but any globally unique number works.

sections.title: Encoding System Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a general format for 6-octet system identifiers with a type field (TT) in the first octet to distinguish different kinds of identifiers. When the type is 0, the remaining 48 bits contain an embedded IP address, allowing a computer to use its Internet Protocol address as its system identifier in TUBA/CLNP. The first octet format preserves IEEE 802 semantics (global/local and unicast/multicast bits) for compatibility with standard 48-bit IEEE addresses.

For example, the IP address 128.96.90.55 encodes as 0x01 AA 80 60 5A 37 in the first six octets of a system identifier: 0x01 marks it as IP-based, 0xAA is reserved, and the remaining four octets are the IP address in binary form.
sections.eli5: The system identifier has a code in its first byte that says what kind of number it is. If the code says 'IP address', the next four bytes are the computer's Internet address. This lets computers use their existing IP number to identify themselves in the new network.
